clinicalPearls: Amyloidosis is a group of protein-misfolding disorders defined by extracellular deposition of insoluble polymeric protein fibrils with a common antiparallel beta-pleated-sheet structure; nomenclature is AX, where A = amyloidosis and X = the fibril precursor protein (p.895).

AL amyloidosis (formerly primary systemic amyloidosis) is composed of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains from a clonal B-cell/plasma-cell disorder and is the most common systemic type in North America; it can occur with myeloma, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, or Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia (p.895, p.897).
In AL amyloidosis the kidneys are involved in 60-70% (proteinuria, often nephrotic range, with hypoalbuminemia) and the heart in 70-80%; cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death (p.897).
Macroglossia and periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses are pathognomonic signs of AL amyloidosis but each is seen in only about 10% of patients (p.897).
Easy bruising in AL amyloidosis is due to amyloid deposits in capillaries or to acquired factor X deficiency from binding of factor X to amyloid fibrils (p.897).
ATTR amyloidosis is the most prevalent hereditary amyloidosis and derives from wild-type or mutated transthyretin (TTR); it targets the peripheral and autonomic nerves and the heart (p.895, p.899).

The TTR variant V122I occurs in nearly 4% of African-American and Afro-Caribbean populations and causes late-onset cardiac amyloidosis; suspect it in African-American patients with concentric cardiac hypertrophy and diastolic heart failure, especially without hypertension or valvular disease (p.899).

Wild-type ATTR (ATTRwt, formerly senile systemic amyloidosis) is a disease of aging, not inheritance; it predominates in men from the seventh decade and is found at autopsy in 25% of hearts of men >=80 years, and is now the most prevalent and fastest-growing form of amyloidosis worldwide (p.899).

Carpal tunnel syndrome, tendinopathy, and spinal stenosis (soft-tissue disease) can precede ATTR nerve or heart disease by one to two decades, and ATTRwt patients frequently report bicipital, patellar, or Achilles tendon rupture (p.899).

AA amyloidosis arises from the acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A (SAA) in chronic inflammatory or infectious disease and typically begins in the kidneys; cardiomyopathy is a late manifestation in about 10-25% (p.895, p.899).
Abdominal subcutaneous fat aspiration is the most accessible diagnostic tissue, positive in >80% of systemic amyloidosis, avoiding surgical biopsy (p.895).
Amyloid deposits show characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light when stained with Congo red, whereas other regular protein structures such as collagen appear white (p.895).
harrison.pathophysiology: Genetic mutation, abnormal processing, or aging-related decline in protein quality control causes precursor proteins to undergo reversible unfolding/misfolding. Misfolded subunits adopt a common antiparallel beta-pleated-sheet conformation and assemble into oligomers, higher-order polymers, and ultimately 10-nm fibrils that deposit extracellularly in tissues/organs. Soluble oligomeric intermediates are thought to be the most toxic species (generating reactive oxygen species and stress signaling), while fibrillar deposits mechanically interfere with organ function. Fibrils co-deposit accessory molecules including serum amyloid P component, apolipoproteins E and A-IV, glycosaminoglycans, and metal ions. Precursors include monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (AL; lambda subtypes predominate), transthyretin (ATTR; wild-type or >130 described mutations), and the hepatic acute-phase protein serum amyloid A (AA) (p.895, p.897, p.899).

additionalInvestigations: Congo red staining of aspirated abdominal subcutaneous fat (positive in >80%); if negative, biopsy of involved organ (kidney, heart, liver, tongue, GI tract)

Amyloid typing: laser-capture microdissection with tandem mass spectrometry is the diagnostic standard (sensitivity ~88%, specificity ~96%); immunoelectron microscopy more reliable than immunohistochemistry
Serum/urine immunofixation electrophoresis (SIFE/UIFE) and nephelometric serum free light chain assay with kappa/lambda ratio (>90% of AL patients have a detectable monoclonal light chain)
Bone marrow examination for clonal plasma cells (kappa/lambda clonality by flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, or in situ hybridization)

Cardiac biomarkers NT-proBNP/BNP and troponin for staging, prognosis, and disease monitoring; ECG (low voltage, pseudo-infarct pattern) and echocardiography (concentric thickening, diastolic dysfunction, abnormal global longitudinal strain)
Cardiac MRI showing increased wall thickness and characteristic delayed subendocardial gadolinium enhancement
DNA/gene sequencing for hereditary (TTR and other AF) mutations
CT imaging plus serologic/microbiologic studies in AA disease to identify underlying tumor, inflammation, or infection
Electron microscopy of paraformaldehyde-fixed tissue to visualize 10-nm fibrils
redFlags: Macroglossia or periorbital ('raccoon-eye') ecchymoses (pathognomonic of AL)
Concentric ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction plus low-voltage ECG (voltage-mass mismatch)
Easy bruising or bleeding diathesis from acquired factor X deficiency
Multisystem involvement (unexplained nephropathy, cardiomyopathy, neuropathy, enteropathy) in a patient with fatigue/weight loss
Serum albumin <2 g/dL with pedal edema or anasarca from nephrotic-range proteinuria
Atrial contractile dysfunction even in sinus rhythm, with risk of atrial thrombi and thromboembolism
harrison.prognosis: AL amyloidosis is often rapidly progressive; historically untreated median survival was only ~1-2 years, but outcomes have improved markedly over four decades with newer plasma-cell-directed therapy. Cardiac stage (Mayo system based on NT-proBNP and troponin) is the strongest determinant of management and survival; very low dFLC (<50 mg/L) predicts better outcome regardless of cardiac stage. High-risk patients (~15-20%) with advanced cardiac stage IIIb or NYHA III-IV heart failure are largely excluded from trials. ATTR cardiac disease is better tolerated than AL: untreated median survival from heart failure presentation is ~42-48 months for ATTR versus ~6 months for AL. Untreated ATTR survival after onset ranges 4-15 years depending on predominant cardiac versus neurologic involvement (p.897, p.899).
pitfalls: Amyloid typing pitfall: commercial immunohistochemistry antibodies may be inaccurate and some AL deposits bind light-chain antibodies nonspecifically; accurate typing (mass spectrometry / immunoelectron microscopy / genetic testing) is essential because therapy differs by type (p.895, p.899).

Serum and urine protein electrophoresis are NOT useful screening tests for AL because the clonal light chain is often insufficient to produce a detectable M-spike; immunofixation and free light chain assays are required (p.897).

A monoclonal protein alone is not diagnostic of amyloidosis since MGUS is common in older patients; conversely, AF carriers may have a coincidental monoclonal gammopathy, so screen for BOTH plasma-cell disorder and protein mutations (p.897, p.899).

Renal insufficiency can falsely elevate cardiac biomarkers (NT-proBNP, troponin) and nonspecifically raise both free light chain isotypes, so the free light chain ratio (not just absolute level) must be examined (p.896, p.897).

In amyloid cardiomyopathy digitalis, calcium channel blockers, and beta blockers are relatively contraindicated because they interact with amyloid fibrils and can cause heart block and worsening heart failure (p.899).
Interstitial (rather than glomerular) renal amyloid can cause azotemia WITHOUT proteinuria (p.897).
Apparent sporadic ATTRv (no family history) often reflects incomplete penetrance rather than a true spontaneous case (p.899).
Mass spectrometry detects amino-acid sequence variation but does not definitively identify specific protein variants; DNA sequencing is the standard for hereditary (AF) mutations (p.899).
harrison.severityClassification: AL amyloidosis is staged primarily by the Mayo 2004 cardiac staging system (NT-proBNP and cardiac troponins), modified by European investigators to identify very-high-risk patients; the Mayo 2012 revision adds clonal burden via dFLC (difference between involved and uninvolved free light chains). A Boston University system uses BNP and troponin I. A separate renal staging system based on 24-h urine protein and eGFR predicts progression to dialysis at 2 years. ATTR cardiac involvement is graded by stage (e.g., advanced stage IIIb) and NYHA functional class (p.897).
management: Type the fibril precursor accurately, as AL, ATTR and other forms have completely different therapies
Treat AL amyloidosis with plasma-cell-directed therapy such as bortezomib and daratumumab, with autologous stem-cell transplantation in eligible patients, to suppress the light-chain-producing clone
Treat hereditary and wild-type ATTR amyloidosis with a transthyretin stabiliser such as tafamidis or a gene-silencing agent such as patisiran or inotersen
Manage amyloid heart failure with cautious diuresis and careful avoidance of agents poorly tolerated by infiltrated myocardium
Correct the bleeding tendency from acquired factor X deficiency and manage autonomic and other organ complications
Monitor cardiac biomarkers and serum free light chains to stage disease and track treatment response
Refer to a specialist amyloidosis centre and offer genetic counselling and family screening in hereditary ATTR
